claim: Disproportionate reactions to unexpected stimuli in the environment are a cardinal symptom of posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD).
source: Disproportionate reactions to unexpected stimuli in the environment are a cardinal symptom of posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about PTSD symptoms in the abstract.

claim: Neural substrates of associability value increased with PTSD during loss learning.
source: Neural substrates of associability value and behavioral parameter estimates of associability updating, but not prediction error, increased with PTSD during loss learning.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's neuroimaging and computational modeling analyses.

claim: Behavioral parameter estimates of associability updating increased with PTSD during loss learning.
source: Neural substrates of associability value and behavioral parameter estimates of associability updating, but not prediction error, increased with PTSD during loss learning.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's behavioral modeling analyses.

claim: Prediction error did not increase with PTSD during loss learning.
source: Neural substrates of associability value and behavioral parameter estimates of associability updating, but not prediction error, increased with PTSD during loss learning.
evidence: This is a primary finding showing no relationship between prediction error and PTSD.

claim: The interaction of PTSD severity with neural markers of associability value predicted behavioral choices.
source: Moreover, the interaction of PTSD severity with neural markers of associability value predicted behavioral choices.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's analysis of neural-behavioral relationships.

claim: Increased attention-based learning may underlie aspects of PTSD.
source: These results indicate that increased attention-based learning may underlie aspects of PTSD and suggest potential neuromechanistic treatment targets.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the study's findings presented as a conclusion.

claim: Clinical and empirical observations have documented heightened orienting to unexpected events in PTSD.
source: In particular, clinical and empirical observations have documented the negative impact of salient cues on neural and behavioral functioning in PTSD, including heightened orienting to unexpected events, impaired extinction of learned fear, and unstable attention biases toward perceived threatening stimuli (Aupperle et al., 2012; Bar-Haim et al., 2007; Blair et al., 2013; Morey et al., 2009; Naim et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Clinical and empirical observations have documented impaired extinction of learned fear in PTSD.
source: In particular, clinical and empirical observations have documented the negative impact of salient cues on neural and behavioral functioning in PTSD, including heightened orienting to unexpected events, impaired extinction of learned fear, and unstable attention biases toward perceived threatening stimuli (Aupperle et al., 2012; Bar-Haim et al., 2007; Blair et al., 2013; Morey et al., 2009; Naim et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Clinical and empirical observations have documented unstable attention biases toward perceived threatening stimuli in PTSD.
source: In particular, clinical and empirical observations have documented the negative impact of salient cues on neural and behavioral functioning in PTSD, including heightened orienting to unexpected events, impaired extinction of learned fear, and unstable attention biases toward perceived threatening stimuli (Aupperle et al., 2012; Bar-Haim et al., 2007; Blair et al., 2013; Morey et al., 2009; Naim et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Error-guided models of reinforcement learning have robustly shown that unexpected outcomes drive learning by directly updating the value of the cues associated with those outcomes.
source: Error-guided models of reinforcement learning (RL) have robustly shown that unexpected outcomes (i.e., value 'prediction errors') drive learning by directly updating the value of the cues associated with those outcomes (Rescorla and Wagner, 1972; Sutton and Barto, 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to foundational reinforcement learning literature.

claim: Hybrid reinforcement learning models combine prediction-error based learning with a dynamically changing attention modulation variable.
source: A related family of hybrid reinforcement learning models combines prediction-error based learning with a dynamically changing attention modulation variable (i.e., a cue's associability value) that scales with the magnitude of prediction errors previously associated with a particular cue.
evidence: This describes established computational modeling approaches with supporting citations.

claim: In hybrid RL models, trial-by-trial associability values associated with particular cues gate the learning of subsequent outcomes associated with these cues.
source: In these models, trial-by-trial associability values associated with particular cues gate the learning of subsequent outcomes associated with these cues (Li et al., 2011; Pearce and Hall, 1980; Le Pelley, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior computational modeling work.

claim: Work in humans and rodents has identified roles for the ventral striatum, anterior cingulate, and amygdala in encoding prediction error.
source: In particular, work in humans and rodents has identified roles for the ventral striatum, anterior cingulate, and amygdala in encoding prediction error (Rangel et al., 2008; Pagnoni et al., 2002; Garrison et al., 2013) and for the amygdala and insula in encoding associability values (Li et al., 2011; Roesch et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior neuroscience research.

claim: Work in humans and rodents has identified roles for the amygdala and insula in encoding associability values.
source: In particular, work in humans and rodents has identified roles for the ventral striatum, anterior cingulate, and amygdala in encoding prediction error (Rangel et al., 2008; Pagnoni et al., 2002; Garrison et al., 2013) and for the amygdala and insula in encoding associability values (Li et al., 2011; Roesch et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior neuroscience research.

claim: In PTSD, affective stimuli consistently elicit altered neural activation in a network that prominently includes the amygdala, insula, and prefrontal regions.
source: In PTSD, affective stimuli consistently elicit altered neural activation in a network that prominently also includes the amygdala, insula, and prefrontal regions (Hayes et al., 2012; Etkin and Wager, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior PTSD neuroimaging research.

claim: Combat-deployed military veterans (N = 74) completed a probabilistic learning task in the loss and gain domains while undergoing fMRI scanning.
source: Combat-deployed military veterans (N = 74) completed a probabilistic learning task in the loss and gain domains while undergoing fMRI scanning (Figure 1; full task description in Materials and methods).
evidence: This describes the study's experimental design and sample.

claim: All veterans had served at least one tour in Iraq or Afghanistan since 2001.
source: All veterans had served at least one tour in Iraq or Afghanistan since 2001, had experienced Criterion A deployment-related trauma, and were recruited from a larger study by our group examining biomarkers of mood and anxiety disorders.
evidence: This describes the inclusion criteria for the study sample.

claim: All veterans had experienced Criterion A deployment-related trauma.
source: All veterans had served at least one tour in Iraq or Afghanistan since 2001, had experienced Criterion A deployment-related trauma, and were recruited from a larger study by our group examining biomarkers of mood and anxiety disorders.
evidence: This describes the inclusion criteria for the study sample.

claim: 39 veterans met DSM-IV criteria for PTSD.
source: Participants exhibited a range of PTSD symptoms, with 39 veterans meeting DSM-IV (American Psychiatric Association, 2000) criteria for PTSD (see Supplementary file 1, Table 1A for clinical and demographic information); the other 29 veterans had previous deployment-related trauma exposure as assessed by the CAPS interview but did not meet criteria for PTSD, resulting in 39 participants with PTSD and 29 participants without PTSD for primary analyses.
evidence: This describes the diagnostic composition of the study sample.

claim: 29 veterans had previous deployment-related trauma exposure but did not meet criteria for PTSD.
source: Participants exhibited a range of PTSD symptoms, with 39 veterans meeting DSM-IV (American Psychiatric Association, 2000) criteria for PTSD (see Supplementary file 1, Table 1A for clinical and demographic information); the other 29 veterans had previous deployment-related trauma exposure as assessed by the CAPS interview but did not meet criteria for PTSD, resulting in 39 participants with PTSD and 29 participants without PTSD for primary analyses.
evidence: This describes the control group composition.

claim: Veterans showed robust learning in both loss and gain domains, as evidenced by increasing likelihood of choosing the 'better' option from chance on the first trial to near 80% correct after ~15 trials.
source: In both loss and gain domains, veterans showed robust learning, as evidenced by increasing likelihood of choosing the 'better' option from chance on the first trial to near 80% correct after ~15 trials (Figure 2a and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in the figures.

claim: Performance accuracy did not differ between participants with and without PTSD in the gain or loss domains.
source: reflecting this, performance accuracy (% better choice) did not differ between participants with and without PTSD in the gain or loss domains (gain: t41 = −1.29, p>0.1; loss: t41 = 0.459, p>0.1).
evidence: This is supported by statistical tests of behavioral performance.

claim: Including associability in the RL model significantly improved model fit for the majority of participants during loss learning only.
source: Consistent with our hypothesis, including associability in the RL model significantly improved model fit for the majority of participants and did so during loss learning only (Figure 3a; protected exceedance probability of model with versus without associability: 0% in gain, 100% in loss).
evidence: This is supported by Bayesian model selection results shown in Figure 3a.

claim: The protected exceedance probability of the model with associability was 0% in gain and 100% in loss.
source: Consistent with our hypothesis, including associability in the RL model significantly improved model fit for the majority of participants and did so during loss learning only (Figure 3a; protected exceedance probability of model with versus without associability: 0% in gain, 100% in loss).
evidence: This is a specific statistical result from Bayesian model selection.

claim: The role of associability in loss, but not gain, learning is consistent with prior data showing heightened orienting and attentional biases toward negative information in PTSD.
source: The role of associability in loss, but not gain, learning is consistent with prior data showing heightened orienting and attentional biases toward negative information in PTSD (Li et al., 2011; Boll et al., 2013); thus, our subsequent analyses focused on learning variables in the loss domain (see Appendix 2, Supplementary Results for supplemental data related to gain learning and model-agnostic support for the presence of associability-modulated updating during loss learning only).
evidence: This interpretation is supported by citations to prior research and the current study's findings.

claim: Choices predicted by the associability RL model showed high correspondence with participants' actual choices.
source: First, choices predicted by the associability RL model showed high correspondence with participants' actual choices (correlation of bins of predicted vs. observed choices: r = 0.997, p<0.001; Figure 3—figure supplement 1b) and did not differ between participants with and without PTSD (t-test of subjects' log likelihoods and PTSD diagnosis: t66 = −0.33, p>0.1).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis between predicted and observed choices.

claim: Reaction times were significantly and positively correlated with trial-by-trial associability values.
source: Reaction times were significantly and positively correlated with trial-by-trial associability values (κ), reflecting greater decision latency as the associability value of the chosen option increased (Figure 3b; average per-subject regression beta value of reaction time predicting associability, controlling for expected value of chosen option and trial number: .232; t-test assessing difference from 0: t68 = 8.28, p<0.001).
evidence: This is supported by regression analysis of reaction time data.

claim: Associability-modulated prediction error significantly predicted switching choices above prediction error alone.
source: Associability-modulated prediction error significantly predicted switching choices above prediction error alone (χ21 = 323.0, p<0.001; Figure 3c).
evidence: This is supported by statistical comparison of regression models.

claim: Associability value showed a robust neural effect independent of PTSD diagnosis.
source: In addition, associability weight and other model parameters were recoverable through simulation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1c), and associability value showed a robust neural effect independent of PTSD diagnosis (Figure 3d; Supplementary file 1, Table 1B).
evidence: This is supported by neuroimaging analysis results shown in Figure 3d.

claim: Associability weights were increased in participants with PTSD.
source: Associability weights were increased in participants with PTSD (t62 = 4.01, p<0.001) while unmodulated learning rate did not differ between groups (t62 = 0.63, p>0.1; Figure 4a), supporting the hypothesis of a greater emphasis on modulation of loss learning by attention in PTSD.
evidence: This is supported by statistical comparison of model parameters between groups.

claim: Unmodulated learning rate did not differ between participants with and without PTSD.
source: Associability weights were increased in participants with PTSD (t62 = 4.01, p<0.001) while unmodulated learning rate did not differ between groups (t62 = 0.63, p>0.1; Figure 4a), supporting the hypothesis of a greater emphasis on modulation of loss learning by attention in PTSD.
evidence: This is supported by statistical comparison of model parameters between groups.

claim: Participants with PTSD had significantly higher associability weights compared to MDD-only participants.
source: Compared to MDD-only participants, the participants with PTSD had significantly higher associability weights (t57 = 7.25, p<0.001) but similar unmodulated learning rates (t57 = 1.44, p>0.1).
evidence: This is supported by statistical comparison with a separate MDD cohort.

claim: Participants with PTSD had similar unmodulated learning rates compared to MDD-only participants.
source: Compared to MDD-only participants, the participants with PTSD had significantly higher associability weights (t57 = 7.25, p<0.001) but similar unmodulated learning rates (t57 = 1.44, p>0.1).
evidence: This is supported by statistical comparison with a separate MDD cohort.

claim: Increased associability-modulated learning appears specific to PTSD and not to mood-related psychopathology.
source: Therefore, despite the high comorbidity between PTSD and depression (O'Donnell et al., 2004), increased associability-modulated learning appears specific to PTSD and not to mood-related psychopathology.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison with MDD participants and cited literature on comorbidity.

claim: Neural encoding of associability values showed a significant relationship with PTSD at an FDR-corrected whole brain significance level in a network of regions including bilateral amygdala and insula.
source: Corroborating the behavioral findings of greater associability value updating in participants with PTSD, neural encoding of associability values showed a significant relationship with PTSD at an FDR-corrected whole brain significance level in a network of regions including bilateral amygdala and insula, hypothesized areas of relevance for PTSD and associability-based learning (Pitman et al., 2012; Li et al., 2011) (Figure 4b; Supplementary file 1, Table 1C; see Figure 3d for associability-related signaling across participants after accounting for PTSD and covariates).
evidence: This is supported by whole-brain neuroimaging analysis results shown in Figure 4b.

claim: PTSD was significantly related to associability-related activation in amygdala and insula anatomical regions of interest.
source: To further test the localization of the increased associability-related activation in PTSD to our a priori hypothesized areas of amygdala and insula, we extracted beta values from these anatomical regions of interest (see Materials and methods for ROI definition). PTSD was significantly related to associability-related activation in these areas (amygdala: t37 = 2.45, p<0.05; insula: t37 = 3.87, p<0.001).
evidence: This is supported by ROI analysis of neuroimaging data.

claim: Replacing the binary PTSD diagnosis with a dimensional measure of PTSD symptom severity resulted in a similar pattern of effects.
source: Replacing the binary PTSD diagnosis with a dimensional measure of PTSD symptom severity (total CAPS score) across all veteran participants resulted in a similar pattern of effects (Figure 5a; Supplementary file 1, Table 1D).
evidence: This is supported by additional analysis using continuous PTSD severity scores.

claim: PTSD was not related to neural responses to prediction error at the whole brain level.
source: PTSD was not related to neural responses to prediction error at this whole brain level (Figure 5—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is supported by whole-brain neuroimaging analysis results.

claim: Neural responses in prediction error related ROIs did not show significant effects of PTSD.
source: To assess this possibility, we further investigated the relationship between prediction error activation and PTSD within prediction error related regions of interest (ROIs) derived from a trauma-unexposed reference cohort, separate from the veteran cohort (described in Materials and methods). Neural responses in these ROIs (including ventral striatum and vmPFC) also did not show significant effects of PTSD for prediction error, even in neural regions strongly related to prediction error signaling (see Materials and methods for details; reference group prediction error activation is shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by ROI analysis of neuroimaging data.

claim: Participants showed significant prediction error activation in striatum independent of PTSD.
source: Independent of PTSD, participants showed significant prediction error activation in striatum (left striatum: t42 = 3.56, p<0.001; right striatum: t42 = 3.02, p<.005), further supporting intact PE-related signal that is unaffected by PTSD.
evidence: This is supported by statistical tests of neural activation in striatum ROIs.

claim: The hyperarousal and avoidance/numbing symptom clusters showed the most extensive neural responses corresponding with associability.
source: The hyperarousal and avoidance/numbing symptom clusters showed the most extensive neural responses corresponding with associability (Figure 5a; Supplementary file 1,Tables 2E and 2F), with little relationship with re-experiencing symptoms (Figure 5a; Supplementary file 1, Table 2G).
evidence: This is supported by symptom cluster analysis of neuroimaging data shown in Figure 5a.

claim: Re-experiencing symptoms showed little relationship with neural responses corresponding with associability.
source: The hyperarousal and avoidance/numbing symptom clusters showed the most extensive neural responses corresponding with associability (Figure 5a; Supplementary file 1,Tables 2E and 2F), with little relationship with re-experiencing symptoms (Figure 5a; Supplementary file 1, Table 2G).
evidence: This is supported by symptom cluster analysis of neuroimaging data shown in Figure 5a.

claim: The addition of PTSD diagnosis significantly improved model fit for bilateral amygdala in predicting switching behavior.
source: The addition of PTSD diagnosis, hyperarousal symptoms, and avoidance/numbing symptoms each significantly improved model fit for bilateral amygdala after accounting for multiple comparisons (αBonferroni =.006; PTSD diagnosis:χ22 = 12.5 p<.005; hyperarousal: χ22 = 12.6, p<.005; avoidance/numbing: χ22 = 12.0, p<.005; Figure 5b), while re-experiencing symptoms did not (χ22 = 6.0, p>0.01; similar patterns were observed for bilateral insula; Figure 5—figure supplement 1b and c).
evidence: This is supported by hierarchical logistic regression analysis results shown in Figure 5b.

claim: The addition of hyperarousal symptoms significantly improved model fit for bilateral amygdala in predicting switching behavior.
source: The addition of PTSD diagnosis, hyperarousal symptoms, and avoidance/numbing symptoms each significantly improved model fit for bilateral amygdala after accounting for multiple comparisons (αBonferroni =.006; PTSD diagnosis:χ22 = 12.5 p<.005; hyperarousal: χ22 = 12.6, p<.005; avoidance/numbing: χ22 = 12.0, p<.005; Figure 5b), while re-experiencing symptoms did not (χ22 = 6.0, p>0.01; similar patterns were observed for bilateral insula; Figure 5—figure supplement 1b and c).
evidence: This is supported by hierarchical logistic regression analysis results shown in Figure 5b.

claim: The addition of avoidance/numbing symptoms significantly improved model fit for bilateral amygdala in predicting switching behavior.
source: The addition of PTSD diagnosis, hyperarousal symptoms, and avoidance/numbing symptoms each significantly improved model fit for bilateral amygdala after accounting for multiple comparisons (αBonferroni =.006; PTSD diagnosis:χ22 = 12.5 p<.005; hyperarousal: χ22 = 12.6, p<.005; avoidance/numbing: χ22 = 12.0, p<.005; Figure 5b), while re-experiencing symptoms did not (χ22 = 6.0, p>0.01; similar patterns were observed for bilateral insula; Figure 5—figure supplement 1b and c).
evidence: This is supported by hierarchical logistic regression analysis results shown in Figure 5b.

claim: Re-experiencing symptoms did not significantly improve model fit for bilateral amygdala in predicting switching behavior.
source: The addition of PTSD diagnosis, hyperarousal symptoms, and avoidance/numbing symptoms each significantly improved model fit for bilateral amygdala after accounting for multiple comparisons (αBonferroni =.006; PTSD diagnosis:χ22 = 12.5 p<.005; hyperarousal: χ22 = 12.6, p<.005; avoidance/numbing: χ22 = 12.0, p<.005; Figure 5b), while re-experiencing symptoms did not (χ22 = 6.0, p>0.01; similar patterns were observed for bilateral insula; Figure 5—figure supplement 1b and c).
evidence: This is supported by hierarchical logistic regression analysis results shown in Figure 5b.

claim: No symptom clusters improved model fit for prediction error-related neural responses predicting behavioral choices.
source: Analogous regressions with prediction error related activation in striatum and vmPFC were implemented to test the specificity of effects to associability; these analyses indicated that no symptom clusters improved model fit for prediction error-related neural responses predicting behavioral choices (Figure 5—figure supplement 1b and c).
evidence: This is supported by hierarchical logistic regression analysis results.

claim: Neither static error-based learning rate nor neural prediction error responses were associated with PTSD.
source: Our approach differentiates between these possibilities, and the data support the latter hypothesis: neither static error-based learning rate nor neural prediction error responses were associated with PTSD, while increased associability updating based on loss prediction error signals increased with PTSD at both the behavioral and neural levels.
evidence: This is a summary of the study's main findings.

claim: Increased associability updating based on loss prediction error signals increased with PTSD at both the behavioral and neural levels.
source: Our approach differentiates between these possibilities, and the data support the latter hypothesis: neither static error-based learning rate nor neural prediction error responses were associated with PTSD, while increased associability updating based on loss prediction error signals increased with PTSD at both the behavioral and neural levels.
evidence: This is a summary of the study's main findings.

claim: The disruptive effect of salient negative stimuli observed in PTSD is related to greater involvement of associability-related learning processes that are based on previous unexpected negative experiences with similar stimuli.
source: These results suggest the disruptive effect of salient negative stimuli observed in PTSD is related to greater involvement of associability-related learning processes that are based on previous unexpected negative experiences with similar stimuli, rather than disrupted responses to immediate cues.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the study's findings.

claim: Animal research has strongly implicated amygdala-mediated, attention-modulated processes in learning.
source: In particular, animal research has strongly implicated amygdala-mediated, attention-modulated processes in learning (Esber et al., 2012; Holland and Gallagher, 1999), and support for the amygdala's role in these processes is emerging in human neuroimaging studies of associative learning (Li et al., 2011; Boll et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior animal and human research.

claim: Support for the amygdala's role in attention-modulated learning processes is emerging in human neuroimaging studies of associative learning.
source: In particular, animal research has strongly implicated amygdala-mediated, attention-modulated processes in learning (Esber et al., 2012; Holland and Gallagher, 1999), and support for the amygdala's role in these processes is emerging in human neuroimaging studies of associative learning (Li et al., 2011; Boll et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior human neuroimaging research.

claim: Evidence suggests that transient lesions of amygdala functioning through direct stimulation reduces PTSD symptoms.
source: In addition, intriguing evidence suggests that transient lesions of amygdala functioning through direct stimulation reduces PTSD symptoms (Langevin et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior clinical research.

claim: The insula plays a key role in associability-based learning and related functions including altering outcome value and computing costs.
source: The insula, which here similarly demonstrates increased associability-related activation with PTSD, also plays a key role in associability-based learning (Li et al., 2011) and related functions including altering outcome value and computing costs (Skvortsova et al., 2014; Palminteri et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research on insula function.

claim: Previously found alterations in neural connectivity and responses to affective stimuli in amygdala/insula may derive from increases in attention- or salience-modulated learning associated with these regions.
source: Previously found alterations in neural connectivity and responses to affective stimuli in amygdala/insula may further derive from increases in attention- or salience-modulated learning associated with these regions that emerges as hypersensitivity to potential threat (Etkin and Wager, 2007; Brown et al., 2014; Rauch et al., 2006; Seeley et al., 2007).
evidence: This is an interpretation connecting prior findings with the current study's results, supported by citations.

claim: Previous work on associability-based learning in non-psychiatric participants has shown a prominent role of associability in learning from aversive stimuli, such as threat of shock.
source: We note that previous work on associability-based learning in non-psychiatric participants has shown a prominent role of associability in learning from other forms of aversive stimuli, such as threat of shock (Li et al., 2011; Boll et al., 2013), which also show disruptions in PTSD (Lissek and van Meurs, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research on associability and aversive learning.

claim: Hyperarousal and the related numbing/avoidance symptoms showed the strongest relationships with neural substrates of associability.
source: Here, hyperarousal and the related numbing/avoidance symptoms (Flack et al., 2000) showed the strongest relationships with neural substrates of associability; interactions of these neural substrates with these PTSD symptoms also predicted participants' behavioral choices during the loss learning task.
evidence: This is a summary of the study's findings on symptom clusters.

claim: Interactions of neural substrates of associability with hyperarousal and numbing/avoidance symptoms predicted participants' behavioral choices during the loss learning task.
source: Here, hyperarousal and the related numbing/avoidance symptoms (Flack et al., 2000) showed the strongest relationships with neural substrates of associability; interactions of these neural substrates with these PTSD symptoms also predicted participants' behavioral choices during the loss learning task.
evidence: This is a summary of the study's findings on neural-behavioral relationships.

claim: The clinical manifestation of hyperarousal in PTSD includes excessive sustained vigilance.
source: The clinical manifestation of hyperarousal in PTSD includes excessive sustained vigilance (American Psychiatric Association, 2000) and resembles what heightened updating of associability values would predict; specifically, reminders of trauma can be conceptualized as stimuli associated with unexpected negative outcomes, with the greater associability updating seen here in PTSD causing stimuli associated with a recent history of these surprising outcomes to command greater attention and increased updating.
evidence: This is supported by citation to DSM-IV diagnostic criteria.

claim: Greater associability signaling during cues associated with uncertain outcomes would create a lack of habituation.
source: Greater associability signaling during cues associated with uncertain outcomes, such as during the early phases of fear extinction, would create a lack of habituation (Norrholm et al., 2011; Collins and Schiller, 2013).
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction based on the study's findings and supported by citations.

claim: Greater associability values lead to reduced learning as stimuli become more predictable, which may weaken retention of repeatedly presented information such as during later stages of extinction.
source: Meanwhile, as stimuli become more predictable, greater associability values lead to reduced learning, which may weaken retention of repeatedly presented information such as during later stages of extinction (Craske et al., 2014; Milad et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction based on the study's findings and supported by citations.

claim: Increased updating of associability values in PTSD may increase the likelihood of inferring new states after surprising outcomes, rather than supporting inhibitory learning about current states.
source: Increased updating of associability values in PTSD may also increase the likelihood of inferring new states after surprising outcomes, rather than supporting inhibitory learning about current states, thus reducing the ability to connect conditioned and extinguished contexts and leading to impairments in extinction retention and generalization (Dunsmoor et al., 2015; Morey et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction based on the study's findings and supported by citations.

claim: PTSD is related to increased neural and behavioral substrates of attention-based modulation of loss learning, while solely prediction error-based learning is unchanged.
source: Here, a neurocomputational psychiatry approach distinguishes between competing hypotheses about dysfunctional processes in PTSD (Montague et al., 2012; Stephan and Mathys, 2014) and shows that PTSD is related to increased neural and behavioral substrates of attention-based modulation of loss learning, while solely prediction error-based learning is unchanged.
evidence: This is a summary of the study's main conclusions.

claim: Participants were US military veterans (N = 74) with combat deployments to Iraq or Afghanistan.
source: Participants were US military veterans (N = 74) with combat deployments to Iraq or Afghanistan since 2001.
evidence: This describes the study sample.

claim: Psychiatric diagnoses were assessed using the Structured Clinical Interview for DSM-IV (SCID) and the Clinician Administered PTSD Scale (CAPS).
source: For the veteran cohort, psychiatric diagnoses were assessed using the Structured Clinical Interview for DSM-IV (SCID [First et al., 1996]) and the Clinician Administered PTSD Scale (CAPS [Blake et al., 1995]), administered by trained study staff.
evidence: This describes the diagnostic assessment methods used in the study.

claim: Participants completed a practice round before entering the scanner.
source: Before entering the scanner, participants were presented with task instructions, completed a practice round, and were given the opportunity to ask questions.
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure.

claim: Participants were provided an initial $10 endowment and informed that payment would be based on actual performance.
source: They were not provided information about the full statistical structure of the task but were provided an initial $10 endowment, and informed that payment would be based on actual performance.
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure and incentive structure.

claim: Participants who switched options in either gain or loss blocks less than 10% of the time were excluded from analyses comparing gain and loss behavior.
source: To ensure participants were attending to the task and had behavior suitable for model fitting (Sokol-Hessner et al., 2009), participants who switched options in either gain or loss blocks less than 10% of the time were excluded from analyses comparing gain and loss behavior (N = 19; 8 control veterans and 11 veterans with PTSD).
evidence: This describes the exclusion criteria for behavioral analyses.

claim: Inverse temperature was first estimated in a model without reward sensitivity, then the RL model with reward sensitivity was estimated with inverse temperature fixed at the group mean.
source: Since inverse temperature and reward sensitivity may not be uniquely identifiable in the RL model, inverse temperature was first estimated in a model without reward sensitivity. The RL model with reward sensitivity was then estimated with inverse temperature fixed at the group mean rather than estimated as a free parameter (similar to [Pessiglione et al., 2006]).
evidence: This describes the parameter estimation procedure for the computational model.

claim: Model comparison was computed using Bayesian Model Selection.
source: Model comparison was computed using Bayesian Model Selection (Rigoux et al., 2014).
evidence: This describes the statistical method used for model comparison.

claim: A logistic regression predicting the probability of switching choices based on the previous three outcomes showed a significant interaction term with condition (loss or gain).
source: To test the appropriateness of this approach, we first conducted a logistic regression predicting the probability of switching choices based on the previous three outcomes, including the condition (loss or gain) as an interaction term on the previous outcome. This interaction term was significant (z = 2.124, p<0.05), suggesting different learning patterns during loss and gain learning.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data.

claim: A model with all parameters separated by condition fit better than a model with parameters combined across loss and gain trials.
source: As a second test of the appropriateness of separate estimates for loss and gain, we compared a model with parameters combined across loss and gain trials to a model separating all parameters by condition. The model with all parameters separated by condition fit better (AICc improvement in 91% of participants, protected exceedance probability of 100%), confirming different learning patterns in loss and gain conditions.
evidence: This is supported by model comparison analysis.

claim: 81% of participants showed a greater probability of the model with associability in loss.
source: Reinforcement learning models with and without associability were then compared within loss and gain conditions separately. 81% of participants (85% of veteran controls and 78% of PTSD participants) showed a greater probability of the model with associability in loss, while no participants showed a greater probability of the associability model during gain learning.
evidence: This is supported by Bayesian model selection results.

claim: No participants showed a greater probability of the associability model during gain learning.
source: Reinforcement learning models with and without associability were then compared within loss and gain conditions separately. 81% of participants (85% of veteran controls and 78% of PTSD participants) showed a greater probability of the model with associability in loss, while no participants showed a greater probability of the associability model during gain learning.
evidence: This is supported by Bayesian model selection results.

claim: Associability weight did not systematically vary with performance in simulations.
source: The mean and standard error of the proportion of correct options chosen were calculated for each value of associability weight. Performance did not systematically vary with the value of the associability weight and the correlation between associability weight and performance was not significant (r = 0.10, p>0.1; Figure 3—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is supported by simulation analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1a.

claim: The model with associability value was a significantly better fit for predicting reaction times than a model without associability value.
source: This effect was confirmed in a mixed effects regression using the 'lme4' package (Bates et al., 2015) in R including all participants' reaction times and accounting for the nesting of responses within subjects. Model fit was compared between a model predicting reaction times from the chosen cue's associability value, the chosen cue's expected value, and trial number versus a model without associability value; the model with associability value was a significantly better fit (likelihood ratio test: χ21 = 8.67, p<.005).
evidence: This is supported by mixed effects regression analysis.

claim: Trial number and associability were uncorrelated.
source: Trial number was included as a covariate in these analyses to account for general adaptation effects; however, trial number and associability were uncorrelated (average correlation across subjects: r = −0.12).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis.

claim: Binned predicted performance was strongly correlated with mean proportion of correct choices per bin.
source: The model showed good concordance with actual behavior; binned predicted performance was strongly correlated with mean proportion of correct choices per bin (r4 = 0.9986, p<0.001; Figure 3—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1b.

claim: The variance inflation factor for PTSD in the regression analysis was within acceptable limits.
source: The relationships between PTSD diagnosis and individual behavioral parameter estimates for associability weight and learning rate were computed in R using a linear regression with additional regressors of BDI, CES, age, and gender. The variance inflation factor for PTSD in this analysis was within acceptable limits (VIF = 1.56).
evidence: This describes a statistical check for multicollinearity in the regression analysis.

claim: Group level analyses were set to a voxel-level cluster forming threshold of p<0.001 and then cluster-level corrected at p<0.05 topological false discovery rate (FDR) for the whole brain.
source: Group level analyses were set to a voxel-level cluster forming threshold of p<0.001 and then cluster-level corrected at p<0.05 topological false discovery rate (FDR) for the whole brain (Woo et al., 2014).
evidence: This describes the statistical thresholding approach for neuroimaging analyses.

claim: Results with permutation analysis were similar to those reported in the main text for the effect of PTSD diagnosis on associability-related neural signal.
source: To test the robustness of our results to the thresholding method used, the effect of PTSD diagnosis on associability-related neural signal at the second level was checked using a nonparametric thresholding approach. Using SnPM13 (version 1.05; http://warwick.ac.us/snpm), 10,000 permutations were carried out with PTSD as the covariate of interest and depression, combat exposure, age, and gender as covariates of no interest. Results were thresholded at p<0.05 FWE, resulting in a corrected threshold of t > 5.36. Results with this permutation analysis were similar to those reported in the main text and are displayed in Supplementary file 1, Table 1I.
evidence: This describes a robustness check using nonparametric permutation testing.
